blocks.html: Every drawing, painting, statue and building is made from a few basic parts. Art teachers call them the elements of art: line, shape, form, space, value, texture and color. This course starts with those parts, then turns to color, then to the ways artists arrange the parts.

blocks.name: ar-design
blocks.cap: The seven elements, each shown on its own.

blocks.html: The elements are the parts a work is made of. The principles of design (balance, contrast, emphasis, movement, pattern, rhythm, unity, variety and proportion) are the ways those parts are arranged.

head: Element
What it is
rows: A mark longer than it is wide; actual or implied.
A flat, closed area: geometric or organic.
Something with three dimensions, or the look of them.
The area around, between and within things; also the look of depth.
How a surface feels, or looks as if it would feel.
Hue, value and saturation of the light we see.
blocks.cap: The seven elements of art.

blocks.html: Names help you see. A cook who knows the ingredients can taste what is in a soup. Once you can name the elements, you can point to the exact parts of a picture that make it work, instead of saying only "I like it."

blocks.title: Naming the elements
blocks.q: A painting has a thick, wavy stroke of bright blue paint along the bottom. You could feel the ridges of paint with your finger. Which elements are at work in that one stroke?
steps: It is a mark much longer than it is wide, and it waves: that is line.
It is bright blue: that is color.
The paint stands up in ridges you could touch: that is texture.
blocks.a: Line, color and texture, all in one stroke.

blocks.html: Mixing up the parts with the arrangements. Balance is a principle, not an element. So are contrast, emphasis and rhythm. A quick test: can you point to it as a thing in the picture (a line, a red patch, a rough area)? Then it is an element. Is it about how things are arranged (evenly, with one standing out)? Then it is a principle.

blocks.name: ar-sort

cards.why: is a way of arranging parts, so it is a principle.

blocks.cap: Sort the cards: parts (elements) or ways of arranging them (principles).

blocks.html: Books differ a little. Some list the principles in other words or add a few, but these seven elements are the list most American art classes use. The Drawing Basics course practices them with a pencil.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)

blocks.html: A line is a mark longer than it is wide. You met line weight and contour in Line Weight and Line Quality. As an element of design, line does several jobs: it outlines shapes, shows direction, leads the eye, and sets a mood.

blocks.name: ar-lines
blocks.cap: Five lines: horizontal, vertical, diagonal, curved and zigzag.

head: Line
Often suggests
Think of
rows: the horizon, a person lying down
tree trunks, columns, a person standing
a runner leaning forward, a falling tree
blocks.cap: Common associations, not rules: the rest of the picture can change them.

blocks.html: Lines do not have to be drawn. An actual line is a real mark. An implied line is one your eye fills in: a row of dots, the edges of shapes that line up, the direction a person is looking, or a shape that points.

blocks.name: design-implied
blocks.cap: Four implied lines. The dashed path shows where your eye travels, though nothing is drawn there.

blocks.html: Line is a mark longer than it is wide, actual or implied. Its direction and character (straight, curved, jagged) shape both where the eye goes and how a picture feels.

Our eyes tend to join marks that line up and to continue a direction once it starts. Psychologists call this good continuation. We also follow where a face looks or a hand points. Artists use these habits to steer a viewer without drawing a single extra line.

blocks.title: Finding an implied line
blocks.q: In a painting, a woman at a window looks down at a letter on the table. Nothing is drawn between her eyes and the letter. Is there a line there?
steps: Our eyes follow the direction she looks.
So the eye travels from her face to the letter.
That path is an implied line made by her gaze.
blocks.a: Yes: an implied line, made by her gaze.

blocks.html: Counting only drawn lines. A row of trees, a line of people looking the same way, or the edge where a dark sky meets light hills all guide the eye. When you trace the path your eye takes, include the implied lines.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)

blocks.html: A shape is a flat, closed area. It has height and width but no depth. Geometric shapes are regular, the kind you can make with a ruler and compass: circles, squares, triangles. Organic shapes are irregular and free, like leaves, clouds and puddles.

blocks.name: ar-sort
blocks.cap: Sort the shapes: regular (geometric) or free (organic).

blocks.html: A form has three dimensions: height, width and depth. In sculpture and architecture the form is actual: you can walk around it. In a drawing or painting the form is implied: shading makes a flat shape look solid.

blocks.name: ar-design
blocks.cap: Left: flat shapes (a triangle and a leaf). Right: a circle shaded from light to dark, with a shadow, reads as a ball: a form.

head: Shape (flat)
Form (solid)
blocks.cap: Each flat shape has a solid cousin.

blocks.html: Shapes are flat; forms have depth. Shading turns a shape into an implied form. Sculpture has actual form.

A solid object in light has a lit side, a shadow side and a shadow on the ground. When a drawing copies that pattern of light and dark, the brain reads it as a solid thing. Highlight, Core Shadow and Reflected Light shows each part.

blocks.name: ar-shade
blocks.cap: Drag the light. The shading moves, and the circle stays a ball.

blocks.title: Shape or form?
blocks.q: Two circles are drawn on paper. One is filled with flat, even red. The other goes from light at the top left to dark at the bottom right and has a dark oval under it. Which is a shape and which is a form?
steps: The flat red circle has no light and shadow: it stays flat. It is a shape.
The shaded circle has a lit side, a dark side and a cast shadow: it looks like a ball. It is an implied form.
blocks.a: The flat circle is a shape; the shaded one reads as a form.

blocks.html: Calling a shaded circle "a circle shape." Once shading makes it look solid, it reads as a form (a sphere), even though the paper is flat. Check: does it seem to have a lit side and a shadow side? Then it is a form.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Space is the area around, between and within things. Artists think about it in two ways: the space on the flat surface, and the illusion of depth.

On the surface, the subjects are the positive space; the areas around them are the negative space. In Positive and Negative Space you drew the gaps between things. In design, negative space is a shape too, and it shapes the whole picture.

blocks.name: ar-design
blocks.cap: A light vase on a dark ground. Look again: the dark areas are two faces in profile. The psychologist Edgar Rubin made this kind of picture famous in 1915.

blocks.html: In depth, a flat picture can seem to go back into the distance. Overlap, smaller size, higher placement, fading color and converging lines all say "far away."

blocks.name: ar-persp
blocks.cap: Three ways to show depth: overlap, smaller size and higher placement.

blocks.html: Positive space is the subject; negative space is around it. Pictures can also create the illusion of depth with overlap, size, placement and perspective.

The cues come from how we see the real world. A near thing blocks a far one (overlap). The same tree looks smaller when it is farther away. Things farther back sit higher, closer to the horizon. Air softens and blues far hills. A picture that copies these cues reads as deep. Showing Depth has more.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: John Singer Sargent, The Daughters of Edward Darley Boit, 1882.

blocks.title: Space that means something
blocks.q: In Sargent's The Daughters of Edward Darley Boit (1882), four sisters stand or sit far apart in a large, dim room. The two oldest stand back in the shadows beside a tall vase. What does the space do?
steps: The girls do not fill the canvas; the room around them does.
That large, dark negative space spreads them apart and pushes some deep into the room.
The space itself becomes part of the mood: quiet and a little distant.
blocks.a: The large negative space and deep space separate the sisters and set a quiet, distant mood.

blocks.html: Thinking empty space is wasted. Negative space gives the eye room to rest and makes the subject stand out. Japanese ink painters such as Hasegawa Tōhaku left wide areas of bare paper to stand for mist. Before you fill a gap, ask what the gap is doing.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)
Grokipedia: The Daughters of Edward Darley Boit

blocks.html: Value is how light or dark something is. A value scale steps from white to black. You built one in Value and the Value Scale. As an element of design, value shows form and light, makes things stand out, and sets the mood.

blocks.name: ar-value
blocks.cap: A nine-step value scale from white to black.

blocks.html: Every color has a value too. Yellow is light. Blue and violet are dark. Two colors can be very different in hue and still have almost the same value.

blocks.name: ar-value
blocks.cap: Tap "Show in gray" to see only the values. The bright red turns into a middle gray.

blocks.html: Value is lightness and darkness, with or without color. Strong value contrast makes things stand out; close values make them blend.
Our eyes rely on light and dark to find edges, read depth and see form. That is why a black-and-white photograph still makes sense: the values carry most of the picture.

blocks.title: Color versus value
blocks.q: Which is darker in value: the painter's yellow or the painter's blue?
steps: Ignore the hue and ask which would look darker in a black-and-white photo.
On a lightness scale from 0 (black) to 100 (white), this yellow is about 89 and this blue about 41.
So the blue is much darker.
blocks.a: The blue.

blocks.html: A picture made mostly of light values is called high key; one made mostly of dark values is low key. High key often feels airy and bright; low key, heavy or mysterious.

blocks.name: ar-value
blocks.cap: The same little landscape in a high key, a low key, high contrast and low contrast.

blocks.html: Thinking bright colors are always light. A strong, saturated red or blue can be quite dark: in gray, the painter's red is about middle gray. Check with "Show in gray," or squint until the colors fade and only light and dark remain.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Texture is how a surface feels, or how it looks as if it would feel: rough, smooth, soft, bumpy, shiny.

Actual texture can be touched: thick ridges of oil paint (called impasto), the grain of carved wood, a woven cloth, sand or paper glued into a collage. Implied texture (also called visual texture) only looks rough or soft. The surface itself is flat: a pencil drawing of fur, a painted brick wall, a printed photo of tree bark.

blocks.name: ar-marks
blocks.cap: Implied textures made only with marks: the paper stays smooth.

blocks.html: Actual texture: you could feel it. Implied texture: it only looks that way; the surface is flat.

We learn what surfaces feel like by touching them and seeing how they catch the light at the same time. Rough surfaces break light into many tiny bright and dark specks; smooth, shiny ones show crisp highlights. Copy those light patterns and the eye "feels" the texture. Drawing Texture practices the marks.

blocks.title: The same painting, two ways
blocks.q: Vincent van Gogh laid on his paint thickly, so the brushstrokes stand up from the canvas. Is that texture actual or implied? And what about a photo of the painting on your screen?
steps: On the real canvas, the ridges of paint can be felt: that is actual texture.
On a screen, the glass is smooth. You see the ridges only as light and shadow: that is implied texture.
blocks.a: Actual on the canvas; implied in the photo.

blocks.html: Thinking a smooth photograph of bark has actual texture. Ask one question: if you ran your finger across it, would you feel the bumps? If not, the texture is implied, however real it looks.

blocks.name: ar-sort

cards.text: A pencil drawing of a furry cat
A printed photo of tree bark
cards.why: is flat paper; the bark only looks rough.

cards.text: Stippled dots that look like sand

blocks.cap: Could you feel it? Sort each card.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Color is what we see when light reaches our eyes. Sunlight looks white, but it holds all the colors of the rainbow. Isaac Newton showed this with prisms and described his experiments in Opticks (1704).

A surface absorbs some of the light that falls on it and reflects the rest. We see the reflected part. A ripe tomato absorbs most colors and reflects mostly red, so it looks red. A white sheet reflects nearly all the light; a black coat absorbs nearly all of it.
An object's color depends on the light that falls on it and what its surface reflects. Artists describe any color with three properties: hue, value and saturation.

Change the light and you change what can be reflected. Under pure blue light a red tomato has almost no red light to reflect, so it looks very dark. Under a red stage light, a white shirt reflects the red and looks red. Our eyes do adjust to ordinary light changes (a white page looks white under a lamp and in daylight), which is why we rarely notice. Scientists call that adjustment color constancy.

blocks.name: ar-wheel
blocks.cap: Move the sliders: hue picks the color family, value makes it lighter or darker, saturation makes it purer or grayer.

head: Property
The question it answers
Example
rows: pale pink is light; maroon is dark
fire-engine red is pure; brick red is grayed
blocks.cap: The next topic looks at each property closely.

blocks.title: Color under colored light
blocks.q: A white shirt is lit only by a red stage light. What color does it look?
steps: White reflects nearly every color of light that reaches it.
Only red light reaches it.
So it reflects red and looks red.
blocks.a: Red.

blocks.html: Thinking an object keeps its color in any light. Its color is a partnership between the light and the surface. Painters who work outdoors see this every day: a white house looks golden at sunset and bluish at dusk.
For the science of light and color, see Color in Physical Science and the Optics lab.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)

blocks.html: In Color as an Element you met the three properties of color. Each one answers a different question, and each can change while the others stay put. The painter and teacher Albert Munsell built a whole color system on three such properties in 1905; he called them hue, value and chroma.

items: Hue: the color family: red, yellow-green, blue-violet.
Value: how light or dark the color is.
Saturation (also called intensity or chroma): how pure or how grayed the color is.

blocks.name: ar-wheel
blocks.cap: Try it: keep the hue, then move value and saturation one at a time.

blocks.name: design-swatches
blocks.cap: Row A changes only value. Row B changes only saturation: every chip has about the same lightness, as "Show in gray" proves.

blocks.html: Hue is the family, value is light or dark, saturation is pure or grayed. They are separate: a color can be light and dull, or dark and strong.

Think of a color as an address with three parts. Moving around the wheel changes the hue. Adding white or black moves the value up or down. Adding a gray of the same lightness (or a little of the complement) lowers the saturation without changing the value much.

head: Color
Hue
Value
Saturation
blocks.cap: Five colors described by their three properties.

blocks.title: What changed?
blocks.q: A designer swaps a bright sky blue for a soft, grayish blue that looks just as light. Which property changed?
steps: The family is still blue: the hue did not change.
It is just as light: the value did not change.
It went from pure to grayish: the saturation went down.
blocks.a: Saturation.

blocks.html: Mixing up value and saturation. Pale pink is light (high value) and also low in saturation, because the white that lightens it also dilutes it. Navy is dark, yet it can still be a fairly strong blue. Ask the two questions separately: how light? how pure?

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)

blocks.html: A color wheel bends the band of the rainbow into a circle, so red and violet meet. Isaac Newton drew one of the first color circles in Opticks (1704). Painters have used wheels ever since to plan mixtures and color schemes.

blocks.name: ar-wheel
blocks.cap: The painter's traditional 12-hue wheel.

head: Group
Hues
How they come about
rows: the starting paints of the traditional wheel
red-orange, yellow-orange, yellow-green, blue-green, blue-violet, red-violet
a primary mixed with the secondary beside it
blocks.cap: The painter's (RYB) wheel.

blocks.html: On the painter's wheel the primaries are red, yellow and blue; each secondary sits between the two primaries that mix it; the six tertiaries fill the gaps. The wheel is a tool for arranging hues.

The order follows mixing. Orange sits between red and yellow because, in this teaching model, red and yellow paint mix to orange. Neighbors on the wheel look related; colors far apart look different. That is what makes the wheel useful for planning.

blocks.title: Reading the wheel
blocks.q: On the six-hue wheel, which color sits between yellow and blue?
steps: Find yellow and blue. They are both primaries.
The color between them is the one they mix: green.
blocks.a: Green, a secondary.

opts.why: Find the color halfway between yellow and blue.
opts.task: Tap the secondary color between yellow and blue, then tap Check.

blocks.html: Treating the color wheel as a law of nature. It is a tool, and there is more than one. Printers arrange their wheel around cyan, magenta and yellow; light and screens use red, green and blue. Each puts different colors opposite each other, so always say which wheel you mean. This course uses the painter's wheel unless it says otherwise; Unit 3 covers the others.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Between each primary and secondary on the 12-hue wheel there is one more hue: a tertiary color. Mix a primary with the secondary next to it and you get the color between them.

blocks.name: ar-wheel
blocks.cap: Pick two paints to mix. Try red and orange, then blue and green.

head: Primary
+ neighboring secondary
= tertiary
blocks.cap: The six tertiaries of the painter's wheel.

blocks.html: A tertiary is a primary mixed with the secondary beside it. By custom its name puts the primary first, joined by a hyphen: red-orange, blue-green, yellow-green.

Each mixture sits halfway between its two parents on the wheel. Red-orange is redder than orange and more orange than red, so it lands between them. Naming the primary first is a convention that keeps the names consistent: red-orange, never "orange-red," in color-wheel talk.

blocks.title: Make a tertiary
blocks.q: What do blue and green make, and where does it sit on the wheel?
steps: Blue is a primary; green is the secondary beside it.
Their mixture is the tertiary between them.
Primary first: blue-green.
blocks.a: Blue-green, between blue and green.

blocks.html: Two slips are common. One is naming the secondary first ("orange-red"). The other is mixing two colors that are not neighbors. Red and green sit across the wheel from each other, so they do not make a tertiary; they make a brown or gray (see Mixing Neutrals).

blocks.name: ar-wheel
blocks.cap: P for primary, S for secondary, T for tertiary: every T sits between a P and an S.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Painters change a color's value and saturation by adding white, black or gray. Each has its own name.

blocks.name: ar-wheel
blocks.cap: Blue with more and more white (tints), gray (tones) and black (shades).

head: Add
You get a
What changes
rows: lower saturation (and value moves toward the gray)
blocks.cap: The hue stays the same family in every case.

blocks.html: Tint = color + white. Shade = color + black. Tone = color + gray. The hue stays; value and saturation change.

White reflects all colors of light, so adding it lightens a paint and dilutes its color. Black absorbs light, so it darkens. Gray does a little of both, mostly dulling the color. Pink is a tint of red; maroon is a shade of red; dusty rose is a tone.

blocks.title: Name the mixture
blocks.q: Sky blue is made by mixing a lot of white into blue. Is it a tint, a tone or a shade?
steps: The color added is white.
Color plus white is a tint.
blocks.a: A tint of blue.

blocks.html: In everyday talk, "shade" means any version of a color ("a nice shade of green"). In art, a shade is specifically the color plus black. When the paint is lighter than the pure color, it cannot be a shade.

Real paint is not always so tidy. Black mixed into yellow tends to turn it olive green rather than a darker yellow. Many painters darken a color with a darker neighbor or a touch of its complement instead.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)

blocks.html: A monochromatic color scheme uses one hue in many tints, tones and shades. Mono means one and chroma means color, both from Greek. Light blue, middle blue and navy together are monochromatic.

blocks.name: ar-value
blocks.cap: One hue, seven values: a monochromatic scale.

blocks.html: Monochromatic = one hue, many values and saturations. The contrast comes from value, not from different hues.

Because every part shares the same hue, a monochromatic picture holds together easily: it has strong unity. Its interest comes from light and dark. Pablo Picasso's Blue Period paintings (1901 to 1904) are well-known examples, built almost entirely from blues.

blocks.name: design-swatches
blocks.cap: Row A is monochromatic (one hue). Row B uses three neighboring hues (analogous). Row C uses opposites (complementary).

blocks.title: Is it monochromatic?
blocks.q: A poster uses pale green, middle green and very dark green, plus white paper. Is its scheme monochromatic?
steps: Every color is a version of one hue: green.
Only the values change.
White paper is a neutral, not another hue.
blocks.a: Yes: one hue (green) in several values.

blocks.html: To keep a one-hue picture lively, use a wide range of values from pale to deep, let one area hold the strongest contrast, and vary saturation and texture.
Thinking monochromatic means black and white only. A black-and-white photo is one kind (it uses no hue at all), but any single hue in many values counts: all blues, all greens, all browns.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Complementary colors sit directly across from each other on the color wheel. On the painter's wheel the main pairs are red and green, yellow and violet, and blue and orange.

blocks.name: ar-wheel
blocks.cap: Tap any hue to see its complement straight across.

head: Hue
Complement (painter's wheel)
blocks.cap: Six complementary pairs on the 12-hue wheel.

blocks.html: Complements are opposites on the wheel. Side by side, they make each other look stronger. Mixed, they gray each other toward brown or gray.

On the painter's wheel, each pair holds all three primaries between them: orange (red + yellow) and blue. That is why they look so different, and why mixing them cancels the color into a neutral. The chemist Michel Eugène Chevreul described how complements strengthen each other side by side in 1839 (see Colors Change Their Neighbors).

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Johannes Vermeer, Girl with a Pearl Earring, about 1665.

blocks.title: Complements in a painting
blocks.q: In Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring, a cool blue turban sits against a warm yellow-brown jacket. Which pair on the painter's wheel is this close to?
steps: Blue's complement on the painter's wheel is orange.
The yellow-brown jacket is a dull, darker orange-yellow.
So the turban and jacket are close to the blue-orange pair, and each makes the other look stronger.
blocks.a: Blue and orange.

blocks.html: Picking complements from the wrong wheel. In light (red, green and blue), the complement of blue is yellow. On the painter's wheel it is orange. Both answers are right for their wheel, so say which wheel you mean.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)
Grokipedia: Girl with a Pearl Earring

blocks.html: Analogous colors sit next to each other on the wheel, usually three in a row, such as yellow, yellow-green and green. Because they are close relatives, they look calm and unified.

blocks.name: ar-wheel
blocks.cap: An analogous scheme: a hue and its two neighbors. Tap a hue to move it.

blocks.html: Analogous = neighbors on the wheel. They share a common hue (yellow, yellow-green and green all contain yellow), which gives them harmony.

Neighboring hues share some of the same color. That shared part ties them together the way a family resemblance does. To keep an analogous picture from feeling flat, artists vary value and saturation, or let one hue lead.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Claude Monet, Water Lilies, 1906.

blocks.html: Many of Claude Monet's water lily paintings lean on blues, greens and violets, neighbors on the cool side of the wheel. Vincent van Gogh's Sunflowers (1888) goes the other way: yellows, yellow-oranges and oranges, set against yellow.

blocks.title: Build an analogous scheme
blocks.q: Make an analogous scheme with orange in the middle.
steps: Find orange on the 12-hue wheel.
Its neighbors are red-orange on one side and yellow-orange on the other.
blocks.a: Red-orange, orange and yellow-orange.

blocks.html: Choosing colors that sit together in a crayon box but far apart on the wheel. Red, yellow and blue are not analogous: they are spread evenly around the wheel. Check by counting steps: analogous hues are each one step apart.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)

blocks.html: A triadic scheme uses three hues evenly spaced around the wheel, like the points of an equilateral triangle. The three primaries (red, yellow, blue) form a triad; so do the three secondaries (orange, green, violet).

blocks.name: ar-wheel
blocks.cap: A triad: three hues, four steps apart on the 12-hue wheel.

blocks.html: A split-complementary scheme uses one hue plus the two hues on either side of its complement. It keeps much of the punch of complements with a little less clash.

blocks.name: ar-wheel
blocks.cap: Split-complementary on blue: blue with yellow-orange and red-orange, the two neighbors of orange.

blocks.html: Triad: three hues four steps apart on the 12-hue wheel. Split-complementary: a hue plus the two neighbors of its complement.

Even spacing gives a triad strong variety (three quite different hues) with a sense of order. Piet Mondrian's Composition with Red, Blue and Yellow (1930) uses the primary triad with white, black and gray.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Piet Mondrian, Composition with Red, Blue and Yellow, 1930.

blocks.title: Find a split-complementary scheme
blocks.q: What is the split-complementary scheme for yellow?
steps: Yellow's complement is violet.
The neighbors of violet are blue-violet and red-violet.
Use yellow with those two.
blocks.a: Yellow, blue-violet and red-violet.

blocks.html: Picking any three colors and calling it a triad. Count the steps: on the 12-hue wheel each hue in a triad is four steps from the next (4 + 4 + 4 = 12). Red, orange and blue are not a triad: red to orange is only two steps.

head: Triad
Hues
blocks.cap: The four triads of the 12-hue wheel.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)
Grokipedia: Composition with Red, Blue and Yellow

blocks.html: Artists divide the wheel into warm colors (reds, oranges and yellows, the colors of fire and sun) and cool colors (greens, blues and violets, the colors of water, shade and distance).

blocks.name: ar-wheel
blocks.cap: The warm half and the cool half. Yellow-green and red-violet sit on the border and can lean either way.

blocks.html: Reds, oranges and yellows read warm; greens, blues and violets read cool. But temperature is also relative: a color looks warmer or cooler depending on what is next to it.

We judge colors by comparing them. Put violet beside blue and the violet's red side shows: it looks warm. Put the same violet beside red and its blue side shows: it looks cool. Even within one hue there are warm and cool versions: a red leaning toward orange is warmer than a red leaning toward violet.

blocks.name: design-swatches
blocks.cap: The same violet square in both panels. On blue (A) it looks warmer; on red (B), cooler.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Henry Ossawa Tanner, The Banjo Lesson, 1893.

blocks.title: Warm and cool light in a painting
blocks.q: In Henry Ossawa Tanner's The Banjo Lesson (1893), an older man teaches a boy to play the banjo. Neither light source is shown, but cool, bluish light comes from a window at the left and warm, yellow light from a fireplace at the right. What does the pairing do?
steps: Two temperatures of light fall on the same figures.
Cool light on one side and warm on the other model their forms and set them apart from the dim room.
The warm glow also makes the small room feel close and homelike.
blocks.a: It models the figures with warm and cool light and gives the scene a warm, close feeling.

blocks.html: Thinking a color is warm or cool in itself, everywhere. Violet looks warm next to blue and cool next to red. When you plan a picture, judge temperature by the neighbors, and do not try to label yellow-green or red-violet as one or the other: they lean either way.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)

blocks.html: A color never appears alone. What surrounds it changes how it looks. This is called simultaneous contrast. The French chemist Michel Eugène Chevreul, who ran the dye works of the Gobelins tapestry factory in Paris, studied it closely and published his findings in 1839. Some dyes, such as a black wool, were said to look weak. He found that the dyes were fine: the threads next to them were changing how they looked.

blocks.name: ar-wheel
blocks.cap: The same gray square on black and on white. Tap "Join the two squares" to check.

blocks.html: A color looks lighter on a dark ground and darker on a light ground. On a colored ground, it takes on a hint of that ground's complement.

The eye and brain exaggerate differences at edges. Nerve cells that respond to one area are damped by the activity of their neighbors (scientists call this lateral inhibition). Next to black, a gray seems lighter; next to red, a gray is pushed away from red, toward a greenish gray.

blocks.name: ar-wheel
blocks.cap: The same gray on red and on green. On red it leans greenish; on green it leans reddish.

blocks.title: Which gray looks lighter?
blocks.q: Two identical middle-gray squares sit on two grounds: one black, one white. Which looks lighter?
steps: The surrounding value pushes the square the other way.
Black around it makes it look lighter.
White around it makes it look darker.
blocks.a: The one on black.

blocks.html: Judging a color alone, on a white palette, and being surprised when it looks different in the picture. Test a mixture next to the colors that will surround it. Painters often dab a test stroke right on the canvas.
The painter and teacher Josef Albers built a whole course on these effects in his book Interaction of Color (1963), with exercises that make one color look like two, and two colors look like one.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Paint, ink, crayon and dye all color things the same way: they absorb (subtract) some colors of light and reflect the rest. That is why mixing them is called subtractive mixing.

blocks.name: ar-wheel
blocks.cap: Mix two paints. Then try two colors from opposite sides of the wheel.

blocks.html: Each pigment you add absorbs more light. A mixture reflects only what all its pigments reflect, so mixtures move toward darker and duller.

Yellow paint reflects yellow light and some of its neighbors, green and orange, and absorbs blue. Blue paint reflects blue and some green, and absorbs most red and yellow. Mix them and each one absorbs what the other reflects, except the green that both reflect. So the mixture looks green, and a little darker than either paint.

blocks.title: Why blue and yellow make green
blocks.q: Explain, with absorbing and reflecting, why blue and yellow paint make green.
steps: Yellow absorbs blue light; blue absorbs red and yellow light.
The only light both of them reflect is green.
So green is what reaches your eye from the mixture.
blocks.a: Green is the light both paints reflect.

blocks.html: Printing inks are subtractive too. Their primaries are cyan, magenta and yellow. Overlap them and the mixtures get darker:

blocks.name: ar-wheel
blocks.cap: Cyan, magenta and yellow inks on white paper. Drag the circles; tap an ink to turn it off.

head: Inks
Make
rows: a very dark, muddy brown (so printers add black ink)
blocks.cap: Subtractive mixing with printing inks.

blocks.html: Expecting a mixture to be brighter than its paints. Every pigment you add absorbs more light. To keep mixtures bright, mix as few paints as you can, and mix neighbors on the wheel. To lighten, add white, which reflects all light.
The red-yellow-blue wheel is a teaching model. Real results depend on the exact pigments: a magenta-leaning red and a cyan-leaning blue mix a cleaner violet than a fire-engine red and a navy blue do.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Light mixes the opposite way from paint. When colored lights shine on the same spot, their light adds up. This is additive mixing, and its primaries are red, green and blue light.

blocks.name: ar-wheel
blocks.cap: Red, green and blue spotlights on a dark wall. Drag them to overlap; tap a light to switch it off.

head: Lights
Make
blocks.cap: Additive mixing with light.

blocks.html: Lights add: each one brings more light, so mixtures get brighter. Red + green = yellow; green + blue = cyan; red + blue = magenta; all three = white.

Our eyes have three kinds of color-sensing cells (cones), most sensitive to long, medium and short wavelengths of light. Red light mostly stirs the long ones and green light the medium ones. Together they stir both, the same way yellow light does, so we see yellow. Newton showed the other side of this: recombine all the colors from a prism and you get white light again.

blocks.title: Red and green light
blocks.q: A red spotlight and a green spotlight overlap on a white wall. What color is the overlap?
steps: These are lights, so they add.
Red + green light stirs the same cones as yellow light.
The overlap looks yellow, and brighter than either light alone.
blocks.a: Yellow.

blocks.html: Expecting red and green light to make brown, as paint would. Paint subtracts; light adds. A quick check: is the color made by something that gives off light (a screen, a lamp)? Then think additive. Is it on a surface that reflects light (paint, ink)? Then think subtractive.
For more on light, see Color in Physical Science and the Optics lab.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)

blocks.html: You have now met three sets of primary colors. None of them is the one true set; each fits a different medium.

head: Set
Primaries
Used for
Mixing
rows: traditional painting and art classes; the painter's wheel
printing inks; many modern paint palettes
screens, stage lights, anything that gives off light
blocks.cap: Three sets of primaries and where each is used.

blocks.html: Painters traditionally use RYB; printers use CMY plus black; screens and lights use RGB. Each set fits its medium and its kind of mixing.

Pigments and inks subtract, so their primaries must be colors that each absorb about a third of the spectrum. Cyan, magenta and yellow do that well, so printers settled on them: together they mix a wider range than red, yellow and blue. Lights add, so their primaries are the three that best stir our three kinds of cones: red, green and blue. RYB remains a useful, traditional teaching wheel.

blocks.name: ar-sort

cards.text: The traditional color wheel in an art book

blocks.cap: Sort each medium by the primaries it uses.

blocks.html: Piet Mondrian's grid paintings of about 1930 use the painter's primaries, red, yellow and blue, with black lines and white.

blocks.title: Which primaries?
blocks.q: A designer makes a poster on a laptop and then sends it to a print shop. Which set of primaries makes the colors on the laptop, and which makes them on paper?
steps: The laptop screen gives off light: RGB.
The print shop puts ink on paper: CMY plus black.
blocks.a: RGB on the screen; CMYK on paper.

blocks.html: Thinking there is one true set of primaries and the others are wrong. Each set is right for its job. The questions to ask: is the color made with light or with pigment, and what tradition is the artist working in?

Why the K? Cyan, magenta and yellow inks together make a muddy dark brown, not a true black, and three heavy layers use a lot of ink. A fourth ink, black, gives crisp text and deep darks for less ink. Printers call it K, for "key."

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Neutrals are colors with little or no hue: browns, grays, beiges, and black and white. Painters mix most of their browns and grays from complementary colors.

blocks.name: ar-wheel
blocks.cap: Blue and orange, complements, mix to a neutral. Try red with green, and yellow with violet.

blocks.html: Mixed in the right amounts, complements cancel into rich browns and grays. A small amount of a color's complement lowers its saturation while keeping it lively.

On the painter's wheel, a pair of complements holds all three primaries: orange is red plus yellow, and blue is the third. Mix all three primaries and they absorb nearly all the light between them, leaving a dark neutral. Add just a touch of the complement and you get a grayed version of the color: a tone that still leans toward its hue.

blocks.name: design-swatches
blocks.cap: A simple model of orange grayed step by step with its complement, blue.

blocks.title: Calming a bright green
blocks.q: A painted field of grass looks too bright and artificial. Which paint will gray it down while keeping it green?
steps: Green's complement on the painter's wheel is red.
A small touch of red lowers the green's saturation.
The green stays green, just quieter and more natural.
blocks.a: A touch of red, its complement.

blocks.html: Reaching for black to dull a color. Black darkens, often more than you want, and can shift the hue (yellow plus black turns olive). A touch of the complement grays the color while keeping it lively. Add the complement a little at a time: it is strong.
Painters also use earth pigments, colors made from natural clays and minerals, such as ochre, sienna and umber. They are ready-made neutrals and have been used since cave painting.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Look at a screen with a magnifying glass and you will see tiny red, green and blue lights (subpixels). Look at a magazine photo and you will see tiny dots of cyan, magenta, yellow and black ink, called a halftone. From a normal distance, the eye blends both into smooth color.

blocks.name: design-screen
blocks.cap: The same orange from a distance, on a screen up close, and in print up close.

blocks.html: A screen adds red, green and blue light. A printer subtracts with cyan, magenta, yellow and black dots on white paper. The two can show different ranges of colors.

A screen makes yellow by lighting its red and green subpixels; a printer makes red by overlapping magenta and yellow dots. The range of colors a device can show is called its gamut. Some glowing screen colors, especially very bright greens, blues and oranges, lie outside what inks can reach on paper, so they print duller.

blocks.title: Two ways to make red
blocks.q: How does a screen make red, and how does a printer make red?
steps: A screen gives off light: it lights its red subpixels and leaves green and blue dark.
A printer subtracts: magenta ink absorbs green light and yellow ink absorbs blue light.
Together the two inks leave mostly red light to bounce back from the paper.
blocks.a: Screen: red light alone. Printer: magenta and yellow ink.

blocks.html: Expecting a bright screen color to print exactly the same. The screen glows; paper only reflects. Designers check colors in print-preview modes, choose inks for special jobs, and expect the brightest screen colors to come out a little quieter on paper.
Painters found a related idea by hand. Georges Seurat placed small dots of color side by side so they would blend in the viewer's eye (see Seurat and Pointillism).

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)

blocks.html: The elements are the parts; the principles of design are the ways artists arrange them. The first is balance: how the visual weight is spread across a work. You met it in Balance in Drawing Basics.

blocks.name: ar-design
blocks.cap: Symmetrical, asymmetrical and radial balance.

items: Symmetrical: the two halves mirror each other. It feels formal, stable and calm.
Asymmetrical: the halves differ but still feel even, like a seesaw with a big child near the middle and a small child at the far end.
Radial: parts spread out from a center, like spokes of a wheel or petals of a flower.

blocks.html: Balance is how visual weight is spread: symmetrical, asymmetrical or radial. Unequal things can balance when their visual weights even out.

Some things pull the eye harder than others; we say they have more visual weight. Larger size, darker value or stronger contrast, brighter saturation, more detail or texture, and isolation all add weight. A shape far from the center also counts for more, as on a seesaw. So a small, dark, detailed shape near one edge can balance a large, pale, plain shape near the middle.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: James McNeill Whistler, Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1, 1871.

blocks.title: Balance without mirror halves
blocks.q: Whistler titled his famous portrait of his mother Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1 (1871). She sits in profile on the right side of the canvas. A dark curtain hangs at the left, and a framed picture hangs on the wall. What kind of balance is this?
steps: The two halves do not mirror each other.
The dark curtain and the framed picture on the left give weight that answers the large seated figure on the right.
Unequal parts that still feel even make asymmetrical balance.
blocks.a: Asymmetrical balance.

blocks.html: Buildings and objects show all three kinds. The Taj Mahal (1632 to 1653) is famously symmetrical. The north rose window of Chartres Cathedral is radial: its panes spread from a center. Many carpets, such as the Ardabil Carpet (1539 to 1540), are built around a central medallion.

Thinking only mirror symmetry balances. Asymmetrical balance is everywhere in painting and photography, and often feels more lively. Test it by covering one side: if the picture suddenly tips, the two sides were balancing each other.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Contrast puts unlike things side by side. The bigger the difference, the stronger the contrast. Contrast wakes a picture up and helps parts stand apart.

blocks.name: ar-design
blocks.cap: Contrast of value (light and dark), of shape and color, and a textured surface that would contrast with a smooth one.

head: Kind of contrast
Example
rows: a white boat on a dark sea
complements side by side: an orange buoy on blue water
warm firelight in a cool blue room
one bright red umbrella in a gray street
a tiny figure beside a huge mountain
a round moon above jagged rooftops
one leaning post in a row of upright ones
blocks.cap: Contrast can come from any element.

blocks.html: Contrast is any strong difference: light and dark, big and small, rough and smooth, warm and cool, bright and dull, round and angular.

Our eyes are built to notice differences. A sameness fades into the background; a difference grabs attention. That is why contrast is the main tool for emphasis, and why too little contrast can make a picture feel flat.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Fan Kuan, Travelers among Mountains and Streams, about 1000.

blocks.title: Contrast of size
blocks.q: In Fan Kuan's Travelers among Mountains and Streams (about 1000), a towering mountain fills most of the scroll. A small train of travelers with pack mules moves along the road near the bottom. What kind of contrast is strongest, and what does it suggest?
steps: The mountain is huge; the travelers are tiny.
That is a contrast of size (scale).
It makes nature feel vast and people small within it.
blocks.a: Size: the tiny travelers make the mountain feel immense.

blocks.html: Thinking contrast means only black against white. Value contrast is the strongest kind in many pictures, but any strong difference counts: a smooth sphere on rough sand, a single warm color among cool ones, a tiny shape beside a big one.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)
University of Washington, A Visual Sourcebook of Chinese Civilization: Northern Song Landscape Painting

blocks.html: Emphasis makes one part stand out, so the viewer knows where to look first. That part is the focal point. A picture can have smaller accents too, but one area should lead. You placed focal points in The Focal Point.

blocks.name: ar-design
blocks.cap: Many small gray circles and one larger red one: the red circle is the focal point.

items: Contrast: the lightest light against the darkest dark, or the one bright color.
Isolation: one thing set apart from a group.
Placement: at the center, or where lines and gazes meet.

blocks.html: Emphasis creates a focal point through contrast, isolation, placement, detail or lines that lead to it. Artists often combine several.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Leonardo da Vinci, The Last Supper, about 1495 to 1498.

blocks.title: Emphasis in The Last Supper
blocks.q: How does Leonardo make Christ the focal point of The Last Supper (about 1495 to 1498)?
steps: Placement: Christ sits at the center of the long table.
Convergence: the lines of the ceiling, walls and table all lead to a vanishing point at his head (one-point perspective; see Linear Perspective).
Isolation and contrast: the apostles cluster in groups, while he sits apart, framed by the bright window behind him.
blocks.a: Central placement, converging lines, isolation and a bright window behind his head.

blocks.html: Each tool works on the same habit of the eye: we look first at what is different and at where directions point. When several tools agree on one spot, the emphasis is strong and the picture reads quickly.

Light can do the same job. In Rembrandt's The Night Watch (1642), light falls on the captain and his lieutenant in the middle of a crowd. In Caravaggio's The Calling of Saint Matthew (1599 to 1600), a beam of light crosses a dark room to the men at a table, in the direction Christ points. (Which man is Matthew is debated.)

Emphasizing several things equally: every figure bright, every corner detailed. Then nothing stands out and the eye wanders. Choose one star, and let the rest support it with less contrast and less detail.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)
Wikipedia: The Calling of Saint Matthew (no Grokipedia page)

blocks.html: In design, movement is the path the viewer's eye travels through a work. Artists build that path with lines (actual and implied), edges, repeated colors and shapes, gazes, and shapes that point.

blocks.name: ar-design
blocks.cap: A curving line and a row of pointed shapes carry the eye from lower left to upper right.

blocks.html: Movement is the path the eye follows: led by lines, edges, shapes, repeated colors and gazes, usually toward the focal point.

Once the eye lands, it follows the strongest direction it finds: along an edge, around a curve, from one patch of red to the next. A good path keeps the eye inside the picture and brings it back to the focal point. Leading Lines practices this.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Katsushika Hokusai, Under the Wave off Kanagawa (The Great Wave), about 1830 to 1832.

blocks.title: Following the eye in The Great Wave
blocks.q: Describe the path the eye takes through Hokusai's Great Wave (about 1830 to 1832).
steps: The eye catches the huge curve of the wave on the left.
It rides the curve up to the clawed crest, then down onto the boats.
Inside the curve sits a small Mount Fuji, where the eye comes to rest.
blocks.a: Along the curve of the wave, down to the boats, and into the hollow where Fuji sits.

blocks.html: Other paintings move the eye differently. In Bruegel's Hunters in the Snow (1565), the hunters, trees and slope form a diagonal that carries the eye down from the left into the valley. In van Gogh's The Starry Night (1889), the eye swirls through the curving sky.

Thinking movement means a picture of something moving. A galloping horse may sit still on the canvas, while a quiet still life can have strong movement if its edges and colors lead the eye around. In design, movement is about the viewer's eye.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)
Grokipedia: The Great Wave off Kanagawa
Grokipedia: The Hunters in the Snow

blocks.html: A pattern repeats a motif (a shape, line, color or small design) in a regular way across a surface. You find patterns in fabric, tiles, wallpaper, baskets and in nature.

blocks.name: ar-pattern
blocks.cap: A motif pair, one circle and two diamonds, repeated: an ABB pattern.

blocks.html: Pattern = a motif repeated regularly. Find the smallest unit that repeats; that unit is the motif.
Repeating a motif gives a surface order and unity, and our eyes enjoy finding the rule. A small change in the rule (a different color every third motif) is enough to make a new pattern.

blocks.name: ar-pattern
blocks.cap: An eight-pointed star pattern, a design found across Islamic art.

blocks.html: Islamic artists built rich patterns from geometry, as in Geometry, Arabesque and Calligraphy. Asante weavers in Ghana make kente cloth from narrow woven strips sewn edge to edge, each strip carrying repeating blocks of pattern. The Book of Kells (about 800) fills its pages with knots and spirals.

blocks.title: Find the motif
blocks.q: A border repeats: red star, red star, yellow heart, red star, red star, yellow heart, … What is the motif, and what kind of repeat is it?
steps: Look for the shortest group that repeats: red star, red star, yellow heart.
Two of the first, one of the second: AAB.
blocks.a: The motif is two red stars and a yellow heart, an AAB pattern.

blocks.html: Using pattern and rhythm as the same word. A pattern is the repeated motif and its rule. Rhythm (the next topic) is the sense of beat or flow that the spacing of repeats creates. A pattern usually has rhythm, but you can have rhythm without a strict pattern.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)

blocks.html: In music, rhythm is a beat. In design, rhythm is a visual beat made by repeating elements with spaces between them. The spacing and the way the repeats change set the kind of rhythm.

blocks.name: ar-pattern
blocks.cap: Four rhythms: regular, alternating, progressive and flowing.

head: Rhythm
How it works
Think of
rows: the same element, the same spacing
stripes of two colors; brick and stone
each repeat changes a little, step by step
repeats follow a curving, wavelike path
blocks.cap: Four common kinds of visual rhythm.

blocks.html: Rhythm is a beat made by repetition and spacing: regular, alternating, progressive or flowing.

The eye jumps from one repeat to the next, like a foot tapping to music. Even spacing feels steady; turns between two elements feel like a march; gradual change feels like growth or motion toward something.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Prayer hall, Great Mosque of Córdoba, begun 785.

blocks.title: Rhythm in architecture
blocks.q: In the prayer hall of the Great Mosque of Córdoba, rows of double-tiered arches stretch in every direction, and each arch is striped with alternating wedges of red brick and white stone. What kinds of rhythm are there?
steps: Arch after arch with the same spacing: a regular rhythm.
Red and white wedges taking turns in each arch: an alternating rhythm.
blocks.a: A regular rhythm of arches and an alternating rhythm of red and white.

blocks.html: Thinking rhythm needs exact repeats. A progressive rhythm changes step by step, like circles that grow or a row of trees shrinking into the distance. Ask: is there a beat the eye follows from one to the next? Then there is rhythm.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Unity is the sense that all the parts belong together. Variety is the differences that keep a work interesting. The two pull against each other, and good design balances them.

blocks.name: ar-design
blocks.cap: Unity, variety, too much sameness, and too much variety.

blocks.html: Unity ties the parts together; variety adds interest. Too much sameness is dull; too much variety is chaos.

head: To add unity
To add variety
rows: repeat a color in several places
change the size of repeated shapes
use one kind of shape or line
blocks.cap: Two sets of tools that pull in opposite directions.

blocks.html: The eye wants both order and surprise. With only order it gets bored; with only surprise it cannot find its way. Musicians use the same idea when they repeat a theme and vary it. Artists often start with a unifying idea (one scheme, one kind of shape) and then add a few planned differences.

blocks.title: Fixing a busy poster
blocks.q: A poster uses eight colors, five fonts and shapes of every kind. It feels chaotic. Name two changes that add unity.
steps: The problem is too much variety.
Limit the colors to one scheme, say three analogous hues plus a neutral.
Use one or two fonts and repeat one kind of shape.
blocks.a: Limit the palette, and repeat fewer fonts and shapes.

blocks.html: Thinking unity means everything the same. Rows of identical gray squares are unified, and dull. Unity is about belonging together; it leaves room for differences in size, value, and a well-placed accent.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Proportion is the size of parts compared with each other and with the whole: a head compared with a body, a window compared with a wall. Scale is size compared with something we know, usually the human body: a statue can be miniature, life-size or monumental. You measured proportions in Proportion: Comparing Sizes.

blocks.name: ar-design
blocks.cap: Hierarchical scale: the most important figure is drawn the largest, though all stand side by side.

blocks.html: Proportion compares parts; scale compares with a known size. In hierarchical scale, size shows importance: the most important figure is the largest.

Before artists used perspective to show distance, size was free to mean something else. Many traditions used it to show rank. Egyptian art shows the pharaoh larger than servants (see The Rules of Egyptian Art), and medieval painters often made holy figures larger than others.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Duccio, Maestà (Madonna and Child Enthroned), 1308 to 1311, Siena.

blocks.title: Reading the Maestà
blocks.q: In Duccio's Maestà, an altarpiece painted for Siena Cathedral, the Virgin Mary sits on a throne with the Christ Child, and rows of saints and angels stand around her. She is far larger than any of them. Is she closer to us?
steps: Look at the front row: four saints kneel in front of her throne, so they are nearer to us than she is.
Yet they are much smaller. Distance cannot explain her size.
The Virgin is the most important figure, so Duccio painted her the largest: hierarchical scale.
blocks.a: No: she is larger because she is the most important.

blocks.html: Reading a large figure in older art as closer. In hierarchical scale, size shows importance, not distance. Check for depth clues: if the figures stand side by side with no overlap, no shrinking background and no perspective, the size difference is about rank.
Artists also play with scale for effect. In Hokusai's Great Wave, the near wave looks taller than distant Mount Fuji, and in Fan Kuan's landscape tiny travelers make the mountain feel immense.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Looking at art well takes a plan. Art classes often use four steps, in this order: describe, analyze, interpret, judge. The Art History courses build on the same habit (see Formal Analysis: Describe, Analyze, Interpret).

head: Step
The question
Sounds like
rows: "A girl in a white dress stands in the middle of a large room."
How are the elements and principles used?
"Light from the right falls on her, so she is the focal point."
What might it mean or express?
"It may be about who is watching whom."
"It works because the light and the mirror keep me looking and wondering."
blocks.cap: Four steps, each built on the one before.

blocks.html: Describe what you see, analyze how it is arranged, interpret what it might mean, then judge with reasons. Evidence comes from looking.

Each step rests on the one before. A meaning you can point to in the picture ("the light falls on her, so…") is stronger than a guess. Describing first also slows you down, so you notice things a quick glance misses.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Diego Velázquez, Las Meninas, 1656.

blocks.title: Four steps with Las Meninas
blocks.q: Use the four steps on Diego Velázquez's Las Meninas (1656).
steps: Describe. The young princess Margarita stands in the middle of a large, high room in the royal palace, with two maids of honor beside her. At the left, Velázquez himself stands at a huge canvas. On the back wall a small mirror shows the king and queen, and a man pauses in a bright open doorway.

Analyze. Light from windows at the right falls on the princess, making her the focal point. The room is deep, and its lines lead back toward the bright doorway. The upper half is dark and nearly empty, which makes the lit figures stand out.

Interpret. The mirror suggests the king and queen stand where we stand. The painting may be about looking itself: the figures look out at us as we look at them. What Velázquez is painting is still debated.
Judge. Many viewers find it a masterpiece because the light, the space and the puzzle of the mirror keep them looking. Give your own judgment, with reasons from the first three steps.
blocks.a: Describe the figures and room; analyze the light and space; interpret the mirror and the gazes; judge with reasons.

blocks.html: Jumping straight to "I like it" or to a meaning before looking. A judgment with no description behind it is only an opinion. Start with plain facts anyone could agree on, and save meaning and judgment for the end.

blocks.name: ar-sort

cards.text: The sky is painted in short blue strokes.
The diagonal road leads the eye to the house.
The empty road may stand for loneliness.
It succeeds because every line leads to the house.
There are three trees on the left.
The warm house contrasts with the cool fields.

blocks.cap: Sort each statement into its step.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Under the subject of many paintings lies a simple shape that holds the arrangement together. Squint, and the figures and objects often fall into a triangle, a diagonal, an S-curve, a circle, or bands of horizontals or verticals.

blocks.name: design-structure
blocks.cap: Six structures, with the structure line drawn over each.

head: Structure
Often feels
Example
rows: Christ forms a triangle at the center of Leonardo's Last Supper
the rearing horse and pointing arm in David's Napoleon Crossing the Alps (1801)
a river or path winding back into the distance
the flat field and the low line of bent figures in Millet's The Gleaners (1857)
blocks.cap: Structures and the feelings they often give.

blocks.html: Look past the subject to the shape of the arrangement: triangle, diagonal, S-curve, circle, horizontals or verticals. The structure sets much of the mood.

A triangle with a wide base looks like it cannot tip over, so it feels stable. A diagonal looks like something falling or rising, so it feels active. An S-curve leads the eye gently back and forth into the distance. We read these shapes before we read the details.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Jacques-Louis David, The Oath of the Horatii, 1784.

blocks.title: The Oath of the Horatii
blocks.q: In David's The Oath of the Horatii (1784), three arches in the background divide the scene into three parts: three brothers at the left, their father in the center holding up swords, and grieving women at the right. What structures hold it together?
steps: Three arches set up a calm, regular rhythm of verticals and divide the picture into three zones.
The brothers' outstretched arms and braced legs make strong diagonals toward the swords.
The father's swords sit at the center, where the diagonals meet.
blocks.a: A three-part division by the arches, with strong diagonals meeting at the center.

blocks.html: Looking only at the subject and missing the shape of the whole. Try squinting, or tracing the main masses with your finger in the air. If your finger draws a triangle or a slash, that is the structure.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)

blocks.html: To find a painting's focal point, look for where the strongest contrast, the most detail, the lines and the gazes all lead. Then notice where on the canvas it sits, because its place shapes the mood. You used the thirds grid in The Rule of Thirds.

blocks.name: ar-compose
blocks.cap: A focal point on a thirds line: lively but steady.

head: Where it sits
Often feels
Example
rows: Christ in Leonardo's Last Supper; the lone figure in Friedrich's Wanderer above the Sea of Fog
On or near a thirds line
a common choice in landscapes and photographs
a figure about to leave the frame
blocks.cap: Placement changes the mood.

blocks.html: Find the focal point by following contrast, detail, lines and gazes. Then ask where it sits: center for calm and importance, thirds for balance with energy, edge for tension.

A centered subject has the same space on every side, so nothing pulls the picture off balance. That suits subjects meant to feel solemn or still. Off-center placement leaves more space on one side, which gives the eye somewhere to travel, and that feels more active.

blocks.name: ar-compose
blocks.cap: Tap where your eye goes first.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Caspar David Friedrich, Wanderer above the Sea of Fog, about 1818.

blocks.title: A centered figure
blocks.q: In Friedrich's Wanderer above the Sea of Fog (about 1818), a man seen from behind stands on a rocky peak in the middle of the canvas, dark against pale fog. Why does he hold our attention?
steps: Contrast: his dark coat stands against the light fog.
Placement: he is at the center, with the view spread evenly around him.
Since we see him from behind, we look out with him. The central placement makes the moment feel still and important.
blocks.a: Strong value contrast plus central placement.

blocks.html: Assuming the focal point must sit on a thirds line. The rule of thirds is a guideline, not a law. Painters center a subject for calm or importance, or push it toward an edge for tension. Ask what the placement does, not whether it obeys a rule.

blocks.html: Squint at a painting until the details blur. What is left is a few big shapes of light, middle and dark. That simple arrangement of values is the value pattern, and it often carries the whole composition.

blocks.name: design-squint
blocks.cap: Tap "Squint" to blur the details, and "Gray" to see only the values.

blocks.html: Squint to see the three or four big values. A strong value pattern reads clearly from across a room; a weak one looks muddled, however good the details are.

From a distance, or at a first glance, the eye takes in big light and dark shapes before it sees details or even colors. Painters plan these big shapes first, often in small value sketches (see Thumbnails and Viewfinders).

blocks.name: ar-value
blocks.cap: The same scene with four value patterns: high key, low key, high contrast and low contrast.

blocks.html: Caravaggio and his followers built many pictures on a value pattern of mostly dark with a few brilliant lights, called tenebrism (see Caravaggio and Tenebrism). Impressionist landscapes are often the opposite: mostly light, close values.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Claude Monet, Impression, Sunrise, 1872.

blocks.title: A sun that disappears in gray
blocks.q: In Monet's Impression, Sunrise (1872), an orange sun hangs over a blue-gray harbor. The neuroscientist Margaret Livingstone has pointed out that the sun is almost the same value as the sky around it. What happens if you look at the painting in black and white?
steps: In gray, only value is left.
The sun and sky are nearly the same value.
So the sun nearly vanishes. It stands out in color only, which may be why it seems to shimmer.
blocks.a: The sun almost disappears, because it differs from the sky in hue but hardly in value.

blocks.html: Studying the colors and details first. Many compositions work, or fail, at the level of three or four big values. Before you judge a painting or start one of your own, squint, or view it in gray.

blocks.html: When you analyze color in a painting, step back from naming every color. Ask four questions instead:

items: Scheme: is it monochromatic, analogous, complementary, triadic or split-complementary?
Temperature: is it mostly warm, mostly cool, or a contrast of both?
Saturation: strong and pure, or grayed and quiet?
Effect: what do these choices do for the picture?

blocks.html: Name the overall scheme, the temperature and the saturation, then say what they do for the work. Back each claim with something you can point to.

A list of colors tells a reader little; a scheme explains how the colors work together. "Analogous blues and greens, cool and soft" already tells us the mood. The color schemes come from Triadic and Split-Complementary Schemes and the topics before it.

blocks.name: design-swatches
blocks.cap: The colors van Gogh listed for The Bedroom in a letter to his brother (shown here as approximate swatches).

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Vincent van Gogh, The Bedroom, 1889.

blocks.title: The Bedroom
blocks.q: Van Gogh painted his bedroom in Arles three times (1888 and 1889). In a letter about the first version he listed his colors: pale violet walls, a red floor, a butter-yellow bed and chairs, lemon-green sheets, a scarlet blanket, a green window, an orange table, a blue basin. What scheme is at work, and what did he want?
steps: Look for opposites on the painter's wheel: red floor and green window, violet walls and yellow bed, orange table and blue basin.
Those are three complementary pairs: the painting is full of complements, at high saturation.
He wrote that the picture should suggest rest. The flat, bright colors and simple shapes were meant to feel calm and plain.
blocks.a: Complementary pairs in strong color, meant to suggest rest.

blocks.html: Colors can change with time. Some of van Gogh's red pigment has faded, so the walls of the first version now look blue rather than violet.

Naming every color you see ("there is red, and green, and yellow…") instead of the overall scheme and its effect. Group the colors first: which hues dominate, which are accents, and how do they relate on the wheel?

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Colors carry meanings, but those meanings come from culture and history, not from nature. The same color can mean joy in one place and grief in another.

head: Color
One meaning
A different meaning
rows: weddings in many Western countries, a custom made popular when Queen Victoria wore white in 1840
mourning: white has long been worn at funerals in China and Japan
good fortune and celebration in China, at weddings and the Lunar New Year
danger or "stop" on signs in many countries
mourning in much of Europe and the Americas
power in ancient Rome, where Tyrian purple dye, made from sea snails, was costly and restricted to emperors and officials
blocks.cap: A few examples of how meanings vary.

blocks.html: Color meanings are learned. They change across cultures, times and contexts, so ask where and when a work was made before reading meaning into its colors.

Many meanings grew from practical facts. A rare, costly dye or pigment became a sign of wealth and rank. Ultramarine blue, ground from the stone lapis lazuli and carried to Europe from mines in Afghanistan, cost so much that Renaissance painters often saved it for the most important figure in a picture, frequently the robe of the Virgin Mary.

blocks.name: design-swatches
blocks.cap: Five colors with very different histories.

blocks.title: A bride in red
blocks.q: A painting shows a bride in a bright red dress. A viewer says, "That is a mistake; brides wear white." What is wrong with that reasoning?
steps: The white wedding dress is a custom of some places and times.
In China, red has long been the color of weddings and good fortune.
So the red may be exactly right for where the painting was made.
blocks.a: It assumes one culture's custom is universal.

blocks.html: Thinking a color means the same thing everywhere. Claims like "blue always means sadness" break down across cultures. In analysis, tie a color's meaning to evidence: the culture, the period, the subject, and how the artist uses it in that work.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work; Creating: organize and develop artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Design is not only for paintings. Every sign, poster, app and web page asks one practical color question: can people read the text? The answer depends mostly on value contrast between the letters and the background, not on how different the hues are.

blocks.name: design-text
blocks.cap: Four text samples with their contrast ratios.

blocks.html: Readable text needs enough value contrast. The web's accessibility guidelines (WCAG) ask for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 for normal text and 3 to 1 for large text.

The ratio compares how much light each color gives off, its relative luminance $L$, from 0 for black to 1 for white. With $L_1$ the lighter color and $L_2$ the darker one: $$\text{ratio} = \frac{L_1 + 0.05}{L_2 + 0.05}$$ It runs from 1 to 1 (no contrast) up to 21 to 1 (black on white). "Large text" means about 18 point, or 14 point bold.

blocks.title: Does gray text pass?
blocks.q: White has $L = 1$. The gray #767676 has $L \approx 0.181$. Does gray text on white pass the 4.5 to 1 guideline for normal text?
steps: $L_1 = 1$ (white, the lighter one); $L_2 = 0.181$.
4.54 is at least 4.5, so it passes, just barely.
blocks.a: Yes, at about 4.54 to 1.

blocks.html: Pairing colors that differ in hue but are close in value, like red text on green. The painter's red and green here are about 1.5 to 1: hard for anyone to read, and harder still for the roughly 1 in 12 men who have red-green color blindness. Check the ratio with a contrast tool, or view the design in gray: if the text fades, so will readers' patience.
